articles.text: Supt. Jennifer Hawn & Asst. Supt. Ariel Dolowich to fill in temporarily Wildwood Elementary School principal, Melissa Daymond suddenly resigned and departed from the school on Friday, October 11. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich are filling in temporarily until a new principal can be hired. On Tuesday, October 1, Daymond notified the district of her intent to resign from her post at the school. At that time, she indicated she could stay until November 1. Even with a one-month notice Hawn was optimistic that the district could replace her without any lapse in staffing. “Because Ms. Daymond has provided a month’s notice before her departure, we are able to post for a new Principal immediately with time to hire a replacement on or before Ms. Daymond’s departure,” Hawn told Wildwood parents on October 4. However, last week Daymond moved up her departure to Friday, October 11, and has since left the district. Daymond recently completed her first year as principal at Wildwood after replacing long-time Wildwood Principal Carol Cramer, a Piedmont resident, on July 1, 2023. Cramer, who worked for 35 years at Beach and Wildwood schools, said she is not available to fill in at the moment. In her brief time with the district, Daymond supported initiatives including the reorganization of a safer lunch location for students and adding an additional outdoor space for Kindergarteners. “I express my gratitude to the Wildwood staff and families for their support during this pivotal transition. By supporting one another, we can ensure that Wildwood continues to deliver an exemplary education to our students,” said Hawn. Daymond did not indicate a reason for her mid-year departure or why she did not provide the district with more than a oneweek notice. The job opening was posted October 1, and the application deadline has since passed. The now-closed job posting, with an annual salary range of $156,918- $172,928, can still be seen at Edjoin.org/Home/JobPosting/ 2003952 Wildwood parents installed a balloon wreath on campus principal Melissa Daymond’s last day. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters held a virtual forum on October 1 with three of the four candidates vying for two spots on the city council. Participating were incumbent Conna McCarthy, James Green, and Lorrel Plimier. Candidate Nancy Bostrom did not participate. The forum, designed as educational and not a debate, provided the candidates with a platform to provide opening statements and answer a series of seven questions posed by moderator Kathleen Cha, president of the Bay Area League of Women Voters. “You are here today to make smart choices when you vote,” Cha said to viewers of the virtual forum. “It’s important for the League to give the community a voice, and that is why we invited the community to send these questions for the candidates in advance.” The questions included: What measures could the city of Piedmont take to combat crime? How will the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan affect evacuation plans in areas impacted by construction? What incentives could the city consider to improve conservation efforts? What are your opinions on expanding commercial businesses in the city? What lessons can be learned from Piedmont’s ongoing project to build a new community pool? Candidates were each given 90 seconds to deliver their positions on the questions posed by the moderator, and a recording of the League’s forum with the City Council candidates can be found at youtube.com/watch?v=D7XPX9mh64E. “The next step is up to you,” Cha said. “If you haven’t registered yet, you can still register to vote online through October 24. Remember same-day registration is available in person through election day on November 5.” The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is a women-led political grassroots network and membership organization. Members of the Piedmont City Council are volunteers who serve without compensation. The term office is four years, and may be extended through re-election to one additional term of four years.

articles.text: On October 1, the Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a one hour virtual forum for the three school board candidates vying for three open seats on the Piedmont School Board in the November 5 election. For decades the League has hosted in-person forums for city and school elections. Due to concerns of recent outbreaks of Covid cases, the League chose to have a virtual candidates forum. Piedmont School Board candidates Michael Malione, Susy Struble and Max Roman were joined by moderator Jennifer Nixon, a member of the LWV. Nixon asked pre-selected questions from the community to each candidate, and candidates were given 90 seconds to answer. One question was “Piedmont students face myriad social pressures. How do you think the Board of Education can best address student mental and physical wellness while providing a rigorous education?” Struble answered the question by stating the topic of a “toxic achievement culture,” in Piedmont is well documented. She referenced last year’s PHS Valedictorian, Jasper Zietlow’s speech at graduation. “Basically he said ‘I lost a lot by working so hard just to get, what? Just so I could stand up here and be Valedictorian?’ Our students know that, but they work in a world that functions differently, that puts a lot of pressure on them,” said Struble. Another question was, “If measure P passes, how do you think the funds should be allocated? For example what percentage should be dedicated to teacher salaries?” and why what other items, if any, should Measure P fund?” Nixon also asked, “How can the board of education help make Piedmont schools safe and supportive places for members of the LGBTQ community as students teachers and staff?” Candidate Max Roman began his reply with the following. “I think that sometimes what people want is grand gestures and I think that those are fine and good sometimes, but I think that what really makes people feel included is when everyone includes people every day on a day-to-day basis,” said Roman. “I think that there need to be clear policies around behavior, that are fairly applied and clear to everyone, so that people are encouraged to be themselves and to bring themselves to school,” Roman added. The three candidates, all Piedmont parents, have clear paths onto the board. Despite the lack of urgency to win a seat, each candidate respected the opportunity presented by the League to express their views, not for gaining votes, but for educated voting and for the sake of healthy discussion. A reported uptick in unleashed dogs at Piedmont parks and public areas has prompted city police to remind residents and visitors to abide by ordinances mandated in the city code. Piedmont Police Capt. Chris Monahan said the department received a letter from a concerned citizen detailing what was described as “a notable increase” in the amount of dogs in the Piedmont parks for “offleash activities.” The report to police listed two separate incidents near the Piedmont Community Hall and at Coaches Field where the citizen came across unleashed, menacing dogs. No one was hurt in the interactions. Monahan said that the city of Piedmont includes codes that prohibit dogs being “at-large,” which the city defines as “not under restraint by leash, rope or chain. The City Code states “no owner or keeper of any dog shall cause or permit such dog to be or run at large upon any public place… unless such dog is securely restrained by a substantial leash not to exceed six feet in length and is under the charge and control of a person competent to keep such dog under effective charge and control.” The city code also notes that it is the duty of the police to impound and safely keep any animals that are found to be violating Piedmont’s leash laws.

articles.text: Piedmont Parents Network’s first event in their speaker series is on Wednesday, October 23, at 7:00 p.m. at the Havens School Library. Parents and caregivers of middle school students are invited to attend. Guest speaker Mindy Szelap will share insights and knowledge about how parents can shift their behaviors to encourage resilience and independence in kids as a means to reduce anxiety. A question and answer session will follow the talk. Szelap specializes in the treatment of anxiety, OCD, depression, and pediatric chronic illness and pain, utilizing evidence based treatments, including cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure/response prevention, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), strategic therapy, internal family systems (IFS), and clinical hypnosis. She works extensively with families of young children to interrupt anxious patterns before they take hold. Her background is strongly rooted in pediatrics, child and adolescent development, and behavioral therapies. This event is free for the Piedmont parent community and is an adults-only event. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates Week 5 Question Do you think the rigor of the curriculum in Piedmont schools is consistent with parent expectations? Please explain, with specific examples. MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate Piedmont schools do an excellent job providing a well-rounded, comprehensive education, with our standardized testing outcomes placing us in the top three statewide. That said, we must always evaluate the efficacy of the educational experience we offer in terms of 1) how well it lines up with the needs and interests of our students, and 2) how well it prepares our students to succeed in their next level of instruction, which for 94% of them is college. Where parents have expressed dissatisfaction, there’s a perception that PUSD has focused on merely achieving state standards, without enough differentiation for learners at different levels. With over 80% of our students meeting or exceeding the standards, there is going to be a fairly wide variation among them. To address prior practices that have proven to be inadequate, the district has focused on literacy. Elementary teachers are now receiving advanced training and will soon implement a new curriculum. This is a great example of how we can improve curriculum rigor. Time and money are limited, so it’s crucial to focus on the areas most important to students’ SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate Ideally, I could answer based on high-quality survey data. Even more insightful would be coupling parent input with survey data from teachers – the professionals who directly engage with students – and recent PHS graduates, whose feedback would be invaluable, as I mentioned in last week’s Q&A. However, based on informal conversations with a small, non-representative sample of Piedmont parents, it seems most are generally satisfied with the rigor of PUSD’s curriculum. Many parents also appear pleased with PUSD teaching practices, which are critical in bringing curriculum to life. That said, I have heard concerns. Some relate to the curriculum, but some go beyond to other aspects of learning. For example: K-12: Parents have expressed a desire for more developmentally appropriate, genuinely engaging learning opportunities focused on anti-bigotry and anti-racism. Middle School (and beyond): There have been questions about the effectiveness of the CPM curriculum, which teaches Common Core math standards, and a desire for stronger Arts programming High School: Some parents would like to see more hands-on engineering experiences, a greater emphasis on academic writing, and more AP Courses (e.g. AP Capstone Diploma Program). MAX ROMAN, Candidate I think by and large our schools do a great job preparing students for the requirements of college and the world beyond. I think that in certain cases, due to the smaller size of our district, there will be students who want to take classes that don’t make sense for Piedmont to offer, and in those cases I am in favor of those students being able to take them at community colleges for PHS credit.

articles.text: While the pursuit of meaning is often associated with adulthood, research suggests that the foundation for a meaningful life is laid much earlier—during childhood and adolescence. A sense of meaning in life is linked to numerous positive outcomes. • 52% higher levels of life satisfaction • Twice as likely to report psychological well-being in young adulthood • 31% higher GPAs on average • 45% more resilient in the face of challenges • 47% demonstrated better social relationships with peers and family members • 30% less likely to experience depression in adulthood • 28% reduction in risky sexual behaviors among teens with high meaning in life • 72% of young adults with high meaning scores chose careers aligned with their core values • 42% higher levels of compassion and 37% higher levels of gratitude • 155% less likely to engage in substance abuse Developing a sense of meaning helps young people navigate the complexities of growing up; it provides them with a compass, guiding their decisions and actions in a way that promotes well-being and fulfillment. The Peril of a Life Without Meaning Dr. Bill Damon, a leading researcher on purpose and adolescence at Stanford, succinctly states, “The biggest problem growing up today is not actually stress, it’s meaninglessness.” Without a sense of purpose, young people may struggle with decision-making, goal-setting, and navigating the challenges of transitioning to adulthood. This can have both long-lasting effects on their personal and professional lives, as well as presently: • Teens with low meaning in life were 2.1 times more likely to report feelings of social isolation • Adolescents reporting low meaning in life were 40% more likely to experience sleep disturbances • Adolescents with low meaning in life were 2.3 times more likely to develop internet addiction • Teens reporting low meaning in life had 55% higher levels of chronic stress as measured by cortisol levels • Adolescents with low meaning in life scores were 2.8 times more likely to develop disordered eating patterns • Adolescents reporting low meaning in life were 3.1 times more likely to engage in non-suicidal self-injury • Teens with low meaning in life were 2.5 times more likely to engage in regular binge drinking The Path for a Life with Meaning cultivate meaning, we can significantly improve their mental health and overall well-being. So, how can parents, educators, and communities help young people cultivate a meaningful life? Research points to four critical components: agency, hope, self-esteem, and openness to experience. Agency Agency empowers children to see themselves as active participants in their own lives; it builds confidence and a sense of ownership over their journey. Allow children to make age-appropriate decisions, emphasize the power of choice in difficult situations, and allow them to take responsibility for the outcomes • Broaden Choices: when there are seemingly only a couple or few, work to come up with a dozen instead • Respect Their Opinions: Actively listen to their thoughts and feelings without immediate judgment or correction. This validates their ability to think independently. • Offer Choices Daily: Allow your child to make decisions in everyday situations. For example, let them choose what to have for dinner from a selection of healthy options or decide how to organize their study schedule.

articles.text: St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland will have a Requiem Mass for All Souls’ Day on Friday, November 1, at 6:30 p.m. The choir will perform Maurice Duruflé’s Requiem, Op. 9 with organ and orchestra under the direction of Music Director Benjamin Bachmann. Everyone is invited to the Requiem Mass at which we will celebrate the lives of all the beloved departed. Maurice Duruflé’s Requiem Mass is one of the 20th century’s most outstanding compositions and his most acclaimed work. It is based on the chant of the Latin Requiem Mass, a compositional practice which Duruflé helped to revive in modern times. The church will be illuminated with candles, and votive candles will be available for individuals to light. You are invited to submit the names of loved ones to be held in remembrance and listed in the service sheet. Send to admin@ stpaulsoakland.org. The film follows the journey of social scientist Robert Putnam, whose groundbreaking research, titled Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community, examines America’s decades-long decline in community connections. Havens unveiled his Piedmont Art Gallery, which was on the current locale of the Park’s tennis courts. On display in four separate galleries were 375 oil, pastel and watercolor paintings from 11 different countries. The art gallery was a beautiful building in itself, featuring a large sky-lit gallery. The centerpieces of Havens’ collection were 162 large Russian pieces featured at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition. After the St. Louis Exposition the paintings were appraised at low value to dodge custom fees for storing in Canada. Havens purchased them from Canada at a fraction of their full value. John Muir, a lifelong friend of Keith, referred to this piece as “The bible of the Sierras. Painting by the notable R.D. Yelland, Thaddeus Welch, James Gamble and Charles Rollo Peters were also included. Xavier Martinez and Gordon Courts, both Piedmont residents, also had paintings in the gallery. In 1907 Laura Prather Waterbury said of the gallery, “I doubted the ability of one man, unaided as far as I knew, to collect enough art and the kind of art that would hold the attention of both the public and connoisseurs. The exhibit seen in Piedmont is undoubtedly the best permanent display of paintings ever seen on the Pacific Coast.” When Frank Havens died in 1918, the gallery was closed and the paintings were auctioned off. Some went to private collectors, and the new Oakland Art museum. Many were purchased for the deYoung Museum, just being built in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. At one point, Bushy Dell Creek flowed voraciously down a section of the Piedmont Springs canyon known as “The Cascade.” In the 1880s Piedmont Heights waterways were substantial enough for fishing. A collection of streams from Alta, Scenic, The Piedmont Art Gallery featured “The California Alps” which was painted by William Keith in 1879 as he traveled with John Muir through the Sierra. It now resides in The Mission Inn in Riverside. tropical paradise. The park also had exotic canna and orchids, a rose garden, a lily pond and a fountain. The path through Piedmont Park canyon zig-zagged over rustic bridges crossing Bushy Dell Creek. An old oak tree housed multiple raised platforms with seating, capturing the treehouse and safari aesthetic. In 1986, the city enacted the Piedmont Park Master Plan, which aimed to remove non-native plants. After years of renovation little remains of Havens’ vision. articles.text: The Highlanders continued their winning ways on Friday, October 11 at Hayward High where they rolled over the Farmers 35-14. It marked Piedmont’s first game in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Mission Division since being promoted from the Shoreline. “There was some buzz around this game. We moved up from the Shoreline and we’re not sneaking up on anyone. I’ve been repeating that, we’re not a secret now,” coach Jordan Seiden said. It was another big game for receiver Sam Shelby who had 96 receiving yards, 55 rushing yards, along with one touchdown reception and the game’s final touchdown on a 38-yard carry. Tommy Ashton helped open things up with a huge 81-yard touchdown run Piedmont’s first score. Piedmont now looks ahead to perhaps its biggest game of the season against Irvington, another Mission Division opponent. The Vikings appear to be contenders in league this season with a 6-0 record. They won their first Mission Division game 26-15 over Washington, meaning PHS will likely need a win to earn the league banner. Game Recap Piedmont held a narrow 7-0 lead at the end of the first quarter, but exploded for three touchdowns in the second quarter to go up 28-7 by halftime. Both teams went scoreless in the third with the Farmers inching back 28-14 early in the fourth, but the Highlanders added one more touchdown in the final going without allowing any points. In the first quarter, running back Tommy Ashton scored Piedmont’s first touchdown on an 81-yard carry, where he bounced outside to make his sprint down the sideline with 7:26 left. On Hayward’s next drive, Brandon Dicke punched out a fumble and linebacker Cash Elmquist recovered at the 50, but PHS went three-and-out after. Ashton also scored Piedmont’s next drive with 8:54 left in the second quarter on the end of a long drive that stretched through the end of the first, making it 14-0. PHS then recovered a chipkick at the Hayward 36, leading to Elmquist scoring on a five-yard reception with 7:37 to go. Hayward got on the board with 52.5 seconds left, but it was enough time for Piedmont. Starting off at their own 38, Piedmont drove to the house on five plays, capping off with a 15-yard fade to Shelby from Lagios with 6.7 seconds left. Piedmont led 28-7. Both teams didn’t score in the third quarter, but the Highlander’s stopped a Farmers’ drive to its own five yard line when hopping on a poorly handled snap. In the fourth, Hayward scored with 6:38 remaining to put itself within two possessions down 28-14. But with 4:23 left, Shelby dashed their hopes of a comeback with a 38-yard carry on an end-around. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team came away with a big win over rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, October 10. They dominated their Western Alameda County Conference foes 6-1 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center in Piedmont. Piedmont has four matches remaining in its regular season as it looks to secure a berth in the North Coast Section postseason. “That brings our Foothill record up to .500. We need to stay at least even to qualify for NCS, so we need to keep up the good play,” coach Jim Landes said. At 2-2, PHS’ final matches include their second meetings against Castro Valley, Alameda, Berkeley, and O’Dowd. Of the group, Piedmont had narrow losses to Berkeley and Alameda. PHS will host Castro Valley this Thursday, October 17 at 3:30 p.m. when it honors the four seniors on the roster for Senior Night: Emma Eisemon, Carolina Romanczuk, Emma Eisemon, and Alina Shahid. Match Day Recap Piedmont won three of four singles matches and swept all three at doubles. At singles, Kate Jumper won a three-set match at the No. 2 spot after dropping the first set and battling back to a strong final two sets, 4-6, 6-3, 6-2. Arianna Kortum won 6-3, 6-2 at No. 3, while Faith Chin played to a clean 6-4, 6-2 win at No. 4. Piedmont’s only loss on the afternoon was Carolina Romanczuk who lost at No. 1 against Ashley Carroll, 6-3, 6-2. “Kate lost her first set against but rebounded with very steady play to take the next two sets handily. Arianna recovered from her illness and played a great match. Carolina had had a rough day at number one against Ashley, who played like a backboard by how she was returning Carolina’s shots,” Landes said. At doubles, Samantha Huynh and Emma Eisemon won at the top spot in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. Emma Chan and Maddie Tran won a three-set battle at No. 2, winning by scores of 4-6, 6-3, 6-2. Inara Mehta and Abigail Call also won in straight sets after a narrow first-set battle, 7-5, 6-3. “Sam and Emma E continued their strong play. After warming up in the first set, they took the second 6-3. The same was true for Inara and Abby at number three. Emma C and Maddie found their stride after losing a close first set. Emma was hitting some strong ground strokes which enabled Maddie to finish for points at the net,” Landes said. articles.text: Piedmont’s flag football team suffered a 22-6 loss to Encinal. Piedmont High’s flag football team suffered a 22-6 loss at Encinal on Thursday, October 10. It marked Piedmont’s second game of the season against the Jets, where they played significantly better than a 69-12 loss on September 17. PHS was notably without top receiver Dorothy Nemeth. “I thought we played well. We stayed in the game, especially after the first time we played them. They never looked behind and I appreciate that tonight. Dorothy wasn’t here and she’s a main go-to at receiver, so our quarterback Edie Elmquist found her other weapons,” coach Beth Black said. One bright spot continues to be the pass rushing presence by Elspeth Grippando. She recorded three sacks against Encinal and is proving to be a nuisance for opposing quarterbacks. “Elpeth keeps getting stronger. She had three sacks tonight and did a great job at riling up at quarterback. She’s putting pressure on the quarterback and forcing them to make quick decisions. We didn’t do a good enough job capitalizing on that, so if we can change that, that’ll be great going forward,” Black said. Game Recap Piedmont went into halftime trailing 22-0 but didn’t allow another point in the second half. After a couple trades of possession, Encinal scored first with 15:30 left in the first half on a critical 20-yard pass on 4th-and-Goal by skilled quarterback Jazzy Alcantar—going up 8-0 with a successful two-point conversion. Encinal then scored Staff Photos Alma Ruberto scored Piedmont’s lone touchdown in the second half. Defender Elspeth Grippando had three sacks against Encinal. again on a pick-six, running an interception 56 yards to the end zone to make it 14-0 after a failed two-point conversion with 8:40 remaining. PHS’ defense shut down Encinal’s next drive, including a pass defense in the end zone by Dahlia Osman, leading to a turnover on downs. However, Piedmont committed another interception to set up the Jets for a 1st-and-Goal at its own 10— leading two a touchdown with just 1.9 seconds left—making it 22-0 after a successful two-point conversion.

articles.text: In a big upset at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, October 11, Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team pulled off a 3-0 shutout over Alameda by scores of 25-13, 25-13, 25-22. The match was a reversal of a 3-0 loss at Alameda two weeks prior. “We’ve been really working hard in practice for situations that we were put in today. I think we prepped well from the last time we played Alameda and we committed to the plan,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Piedmont’s win showed great improvement. So far this season, PHS’ young roster showed glimpses of their potential with occasional dominant sets, but couldn’t seem to stay consistent over the full course of a match. This time, the Highlanders were picking their shots at the net and frequently landed spikes to the floor. “We were just playing like a team. In the past, we’ve had moments where we were playing all together, but tonight we were connected on a higher level. Everyone was executing, we all trusted each other, and stayed disciplined,” senior captain Jules DeYoung said. Junior Stella Wilks was a big part of the victory with eight kills. “I feel like the whole team just played cohesively. We kept the energy up throughout the whole game, which is essential. In other games, we’ve had highs and lows, but this game we stayed consistent,” Wilks said. Match Recap Piedmont came out of the gate strongly by jumping out to an early 7-2 lead, which included gaining points with two kills from Wilks, one by Charli Panico and Sophie Glass, a block by Mira Sachs, and an ace by DeYoung. From there, PHS extended the lead to 10-4 with kills by Glass and Sachs, followed by the Highlanders pushing their advantage to 14-6 with two spikes by Wilks and two aces by Kalindi Kim. articles.text: After coming off a threegame win streak, Piedmont JV Scots traveled to Hayward High on Friday, October 11 for its first away game of the season. Dealing with multiple injuries, Piedmont lost 28-8 while playing on unfamiliar ground. The first half of the game was rough for the Highlanders. After being held to no yards on the first drive, the Highlanders were forced to punt. The Farmers scored on their first drive on a pass over the middle. After an interception thrown by Piedmont, the Farmers jumped out to a 21-0 lead by halftime. Coming out of the locker room, the Highlanders showed energy to try and get back into the game. On the Farmers’ first play of the second half, sophomore defensive back Owen Curran snatched an interception, taking it back to the house for a 30 yard pick-six. It marked Curran’s third interception on the season and first touchdown. Starting quarterback Jimmy Lagios had to leave the action in the first half due to a head injury, with backup quarterback Jonah Cha-Foster taking over. He helped convert the two-point conversion on a pass to Max Fujimoto. Although the Highlanders had a glimpse of hope, the rest of the second half was not enough to overtake the Farmers They allowed one more touchdown in the final minutes. Injuries proved to be a factor: Three of the four captains were forced to sit out most of the second half. George Saunders suffered a wrist injury, and Fujimoto also had to exit the game. articles.text: An exhibit of painter Mary Lovelace O’Neal’s first return to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art in 45 years remains open until Sunday, October 20. The solo exhibition, “New Work: Mary Lovelace O’Neal,” opened on March 16. In a career spanning six decades, O’Neal has used unorthodox materials and color to show both abstraction and figuration. Her paintings blend worlds of personal details and shared historical narratives, from her beloved dachshund Tillie to her involvement in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Her early works from the 1960s utilized “lampblack” pigment — powdered soot made from burning oil, which she rubbed into her canvases. She used this technique to address three subjects at the fore of art and culture at that moment, which she has described as “surface flatness, black as a color, and blackness as an existential, racial experience.” O’Neal would then inscribe the velvety black expanses with materials including paint, gasoline, masking tape and glitter, introducing an element of play. In time, representational elements emerged from her abstractions, offering new narrative possibilities within a constellation of references across music, literature and social movements. In 1979, O’Neal was hired at the University of California, Berkeley, where she became the first African American professor awarded tenure in the Department of Art in 1985; she became chair of the department in 1999 and professor emerita in 2006. She now splits her time between Oakland and Mérida, Mexico, where her at currently on display was created. Although her paintings begin with a black background, color remains foundational to her practice. Describing the seven 7-foottall canvases on view in this exhibition, O’Neal said, “Painting with color was always a surprise … like dancing with the paint.” SFMOMA (151 Third Street in San Francusci) is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday through Tuesday, and 12 p.m. through 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $23 student, free 18 and younger) are available at sfmoma. org/visit. Mary Lovelace O’Neal, MARDI GRAS UMBRELLAS & FIREFLIES, 2021-23. This Sunday, October 20, is the last day of the artist’s SFMOMA solo exhibition.

articles.text: San Francisco’s de Young Museum will be the sole West Coast venue for the exhibition “Art and War in the Renaissance” this Saturday through January 12. The exhibit will feature monumental tapestries and superb examples of arms and armor on loan from the Capodimonte Museum in Naples, Italy. The dazzling centerpiece will be the newly conserved, complete seven-part cycle of the “Battle of Pavia” tapestries. These colossal woven artworks will immerse visitors in the world of Renaissance politics, history, and art. These tapestries will be on view with original preparatory drawings lent by the Louvre Museum, alongside a selection of 16th and 17th century arms and armor from the Farnese Armory at the Capodimonte Museum. Combined, the works will give visitors insight into the artistry and craftsmanship required to transform Renaissance tapestries from initial designs into glittering propagandistic luxuries. The “Battle of Pavia” tapestries celebrate the decisive victory of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and the imperial army over the French army led by King Francis I. This decisive moment in European history took place five centuries ago on February 24, 1525, around the town of Pavia, outside Milan. The pivotal battle ended the Italian war, which had begun in 1521, and stopped the French from encroaching into Italian territories. “Monumental in scale, tapestries were the grandest form of art and propaganda in the Renaissance and kings and popes spent vast sums to commission them. Yet, few of these great sets have survived and even fewer are on display. The fact that the ‘Battle of Pavia’ tapestries have survived, complete and in good condition, is little short of extraordinary,” said Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco and one of the world’s leading authorities on European tapestries. During the Renaissance, tapestries were the art form of kings, prized by rulers as lavish displays of wealth and power. The works were woven on a grand scale by vast workshops, using precious materials costing exponentially more than paintings. The grand “Battle of Pavia” tapestries were made with silver- and goldwrapped thread, interwoven with expensive wool and silk from across the globe. The manufacture of tapestries was a huge collaborative endeavor and necessitated years of work to produce one set. A single panel of the “Battle of Pavia” tapestries would have taken roughly 18 months to create. “The scale of these tapestries is staggering, as is the sheer profusion of detail. You can find something new and exciting every time you look,” said Jeffrey Fraiman, Assistant Curator of European Decorative Arts and Sculpture, and organizing curator of the exhibition. “But it is also the freshness, the immediacy of them, that hits you,” he added. “These are half a millennium old, and their survival feels miraculous. I think audiences will be awestruck.” The de Young Museum (50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive, Golden Gate Park) is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org/events.

articles.text: This Sunday, October 20, at 4 p.m. St. Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland will present “Con Amor,” a program of Latin American music crossing classical, jazz, pop and folk genres. The event’s special guest artist is Edu González, a singer born and raised in San Juan, Puerto Rico. He moved to the Bay Area in 2010 and discovered his love for singing at the San Francisco piano bar Martuni’s, where he’s still a regular. González will perform with a band with songs including “Cuando Te Beso” by Juan Luis Guerra; “Agnus Dei” by Ernesto Herrera; “Se equivocó la paloma” by Carlos Guastavino; “Dos Palabras” by Josh Rodriguez; “Modinha” by Antonio Carlos Jobim; the standard “All My Trials”; “Despacito” by Luis Fonsi; and “Vivir Mi Vida” by Marc Anthony. González made his singing debut in a 2022 production of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s A Grand Night for Singing at 42nd Street Moon in San Francisco. In 2023, together with a few friends, Edu created “Cantos de Mi Tierra,” the first all-Spanish language cabaret show at Martuni’s. More recently, he played the role of the Pirate King in Lamplighters Music Theater’s 2024 production of Gilbert and Sullivan’s The Pirates of Penzance. Tickets start at $23.18 and are available at shorturl.at/PLOXj. St. Paul’s Episcopal Church is located at 114 Montecito Avenue by Lake Merritt. articles.text: In a first-ever trio tour, violinist Tessa Lark, cellist Joshua Roman and double bassist Edgar Meyer will perform the work of Meyer and J.S. Bach at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall this Sunday. Cal Performances at UC Berkeley presents the trio of Grammy-winning double bassist Edgar Meyer, genre-crossing violinist Tessa Lark and eclectic cellist Joshua Roman for a performance at Hertz Hall this Sunday, October 13 at 3 p.m. This new collaboration brings together three singular figures in American concert music — virtuoso instrumentalists with both strong classical backgrounds and deep connections to roots and fiddle music. The concert will open with J.S. Bach’s Sonata for Viola da Gamba in G Major, arranged specially for this string instrumentation. The trio will then perform the Bay Area premiere of Meyer’s new work, commissioned by Cal Performances, as well as his Trio 1986 and Trio 1988. This engagement is part of the trio’s first-ever tour. “In 1986 to 1988 I wrote a series of three string trios that I premiered at the Santa Fe Chamber Music Festival,” said Meyer. These were the first longer pieces that I had conceived as such, and they set the tone for my next four decades. After meeting Tessa Lark and Joshua Roman a few years ago, I realized that they were perfect for helping me document this personal milestone.” Violinist Tessa Lark is recognized for her mastery of both classical and bluegrass music. She was nominated for a 2020 Grammy in the Best Classical Instrumental Solo category and received one of the Lincoln Center’s prestigious emerging artist awards, the Hunt Family Award. She is the recipient of a Borletti– Buitoni Trust Fellowship, serves as Artistic Director of Musical Masterworks and co-hosts NPR’s classical podcast “From the Top.” Cellist and composer Joshua Roman is known for blending precision with improvisatory freedom. He has performed with leading orchestras worldwide and opened the 2017 TED Conference, where his performance of Bach’s solo Cello Suites became TED’s most-viewed event. His 2023–24 season included his role as the Las Vegas Philharmonic’s inaugural Artist in Residence, alongside performances with several U.S. symphony orchestras. Virtuoso and composer Edgar Meyer has carved out a unique niche in the musical world by bridging classical and Americana genres. Recognized with a MacArthur Award, he has performed and recorded extensively, including collaborations with Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile, Joshua Bell and Béla Fleck. Meyer’s compositions have been premiered by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Boston Symphony Orchestra, Detroit Symphony Orchestra and Minnesota Orchestra, while his genre-bending recordings, such as “The Goat Rodeo Sessions,” have garnered critical acclaim and Grammy Awards. Tickets ($68) for the performance at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall (101 Cross-Sproul Path) are available at calperformances.org, or by phone at 642-9988.

articles.text: As the well-to-do Birlings celebrate an engagement in the family, the festive evening is punctured by an uninvited visitor: an inspector looking into a young woman’s death, in the whodunnit, An Inspector Calls, at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this weekend. The final performance is Sunday, October 20. Questions multiply and guilt mounts as Inspector Goole’s grim revelations begin to crack the foundations of the Birlings’ comfortable lives. Before long, they are all challenged to examine their decisions and consciences in J.B. Priestley’s timeless drama. Eric Birling (played by Myles Kenyon Rowland) is affected by the dark revelations in J.B. Priestley’s thriller An Inspector Calls, closing at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this Sunday, October 20. Filled with Hitchcockian suspense, this production brings back acclaimed director Mark Anderson Phillips (Blithe Spirit, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde) to the City Lights stage. As the U.S. nears the 2024 presidential election, this play is especially timely. Besides being a taut thriller, it’s also “a passionate plea for a more just and compassionate society,” according to The Guardian. Written by the English playwright, novelist and journalist J.B. Priestley, An Inspector Calls is one of his many compelling stories that take seemingly ordinary people in home or office settings and illustrate universally human issues of compassion. After debuting in the Soviet Union in 1945, “An Inspector Calls” opened at the New Theatre in London in 1946. It has reaped considerable praise with numerous revivals and regional productions over the decades. Tickets ($31-$70) at City Lights (529 S. Second Street, San Jose) are available online at cltc. org, or by phone at 408-295-4200.

articles.text: Shotgun Players’ newest production Choir Boy is onstage through October 20 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The play follows main character Pharus, who attends an all-boys preparatory school and is the lead singer for their renowned choir. An Inspector Calls at City Lights Theatre this weekend By Selen Ozturk As the well-to-do Birlings celebrate an engagement in the family, the festive evening is punctured by an uninvited visitor: an inspector looking into a young woman’s death, in the whodunnit, An Inspector Calls, at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this weekend. The final performance is Sunday, October 20. Questions multiply and guilt mounts as Inspector Goole’s grim revelations begin to crack the foundations of the Birlings’ comfortable lives. Before long, they are all challenged to examine their decisions and consciences in J.B. Priestley’s timeless drama. Eric Birling (played by Myles Kenyon Rowland) is affected by the dark revelations in J.B. Priestley’s thriller An Inspector Calls, closing at San Jose’s City Lights Theatre this Sunday, October 20. Filled with Hitchcockian suspense, this production brings back acclaimed director Mark Anderson Phillips (Blithe Spirit, Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde) to the City Lights stage. As the U.S. nears the 2024 presidential election, this play is especially timely. Besides being a taut thriller, it’s also “a passionate plea for a more just and compassionate society,” according to The Guardian. Written by the English playwright, novelist and journalist J.B. Priestley, An Inspector Calls is one of his many compelling stories that take seemingly ordinary people in home or office settings and illustrate universally human issues of compassion. After debuting in the Soviet Union in 1945, “An Inspector Calls” opened at the New Theatre in London in 1946. It has reaped considerable praise with numerous revivals and regional productions over the decades. Tickets ($31-$70) at City Lights (529 S. Second Street, San Jose) are available online at cltc. org, or by phone at 408-295-4200. Cal Performances brings string trio to Berkeley Oct. 20 In a first-ever trio tour, violinist Tessa Lark, cellist Joshua Roman and double bassist Edgar Meyer will perform the work of Meyer and J.S. Bach at UC Berkeley’s Hertz Hall this Sunday. By Selen Ozturk Cal Performances at UC Berkeley presents the trio of Grammy-winning double bassist Edgar Meyer, genre-crossing violinist Tessa Lark and eclectic cellist Joshua Roman for a performance at Hertz Hall this Sunday, October 13 at 3 p.m. This new collaboration brings together three singular figures in American concert music — virtuoso instrumentalists with both strong classical backgrounds and deep connections to roots and fiddle music. The concert will open with J.S. Bach’s Sonata for Viola da Gamba in G Major, arranged specially for this string instrumentation. The trio will then perform the Bay Area premiere of Meyer’s new work, commissioned by Cal Performances, as well as his Trio 1986 and Trio 1988. This engagement is part of the trio’s first-ever tour. “In 1986 to 1988 I wrote a series of three string trios that I premiered at the Santa Fe Chamber Music Festival,” said Meyer. These were the first longer pieces that I had conceived as such, and they set the tone for my next four decades. After meeting Tessa Lark and Joshua Roman a few years ago, I realized that they were perfect for helping me document this personal milestone.” Violinist Tessa Lark is recognized for her mastery of both classical and bluegrass music. She was nominated for a 2020 Grammy in the Best Classical Instrumental Solo category and received one of the Lincoln Center’s prestigious emerging artist awards, the Hunt Family Award. She is the recipient of a Borletti– Buitoni Trust Fellowship, serves as Artistic Director of Musical Masterworks and co-hosts NPR’s classical podcast “From the Top.” Cellist and composer Joshua Roman is known for blending precision with improvisatory freedom. He has performed with leading orchestras worldwide and opened the 2017 TED Conference, where his performance of Bach’s solo Cello Suites became TED’s most-viewed event. His 2023–24 season included his role as the Las Vegas Philharmonic’s inaugural Artist in Residence, alongside performances with several U.S. symphony orchestras. Virtuoso and composer Edgar Meyer has carved out a unique niche in the musical world by bridging classical and Americana genres. Recognized with a MacArthur Award, he has performed and recorded extensively, including collaborations with Yo-Yo Ma, Chris Thile, Joshua Bell and Béla Fleck. Meyer’s compositions have been premiered by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, Boston Symphony Orchestra, Detroit Symphony Orchestra and Minnesota Orchestra, while his genre-bending recordings, such as “The Goat Rodeo Sessions,” have garnered critical acclaim and Grammy Awards. articles.text: Berkeley Symphony will open its 2024–25 season with a concert at Zallerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus on Sunday, November 10 at 4 p.m. The concert will be dedicated to composer Gordon Getty for his long and significant support of the symphony. After the opening concert, the symphony will honor Getty at the Opening Night Dinner fundraising event. Getty has supported Berkeley Symphony for over 25 years, and made a gift of $1.5 million in 2023 to ensure the symphony’s stability as the organization navigated the difficult challenges of rebuilding after the pandemic. The opening concert – the first in a series of four – is titled Stories From Home. The opening program of Berkeley Symphony’s 53rd season answers the question, “‘What does a story sound like?’ “It sounds like Leonard Bernstein’s jazzy, syncopated Symphonic Dances from West Side Story: you can hear the streets of New York and feel the longing of star-crossed lovers,” said Berkeley Symphony Music Director Joseph Young. “It sounds like the whispering breeze of Samuel Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915, or like the crashing of waves in Silvestre Revueltas’s Redes Suite, or the violin soaring over the orchestra, as it does in Kris Bowers’ concerto For A Younger Self.” Stories From Home will showcase soprano Lisa Delan in Samuel Barber’s Knoxville: Summer of 1915. Delan has performed, commissioned and recorded music by Philip Glass, Jake Heggie, John Corigliano, and Gordon Getty. Grammy-winning violinist Charles Yang will perform in the Bay Area premiere of For A Younger Self by Kris Bowers. Yang has performed as a soloist throughout the United States, Europe, Brazil, Russia, China and Taiwan. In 2016 he became the violinist and lead singer of the multi-genre string band “Time for Three,” which won the 2023 Grammy Award for Best Classical Instrumental Solo. “This is music that takes you somewhere, that grabs hold, and puts you in a specific time and place,” Yang said. Leonard Bernstein’s Symphonic Dances from West Side Story and Silvestre Revueltas’s Redes Suite round out the symphony’s exploration of North America’s cultural and musical heritage. Created in 1971, the Berkeley Symphony is committed to performing, premiering and commissioning new music. Subscriptions and single tickets and tickets to the Opening Night Dinner fundraising event are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800. Berkeley Symphony, headed by Music Director Joseph Young, will perform its opening concert at Zellerbach Hall on November 10.

articles.text: This Sunday at 4:30 p.m., the piano trio In the Tradition — featuring Bill Jackman, Michael Jones and Dr. Albert Brooks — will play a tribute to Jimmy van Heusen at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Van Heusen composed nearly 1,000 songs between 1930 and 1970, of which at least 50 have become American standards. Many Americans have heard of classic popular music composers like George Gershwin, Cole Porter and Hoagy Carmichael; although van Heusen doesn’t share their name recognition among the general public, he was every bit their equal. He certainly lays claim to this fame among the jazz musicians who continue to play the many timeless tunes that he composed. These songs include jazz standards such as “Polka Dots and Moonbeams” (1940) and “Like Someone in Love” (1944). Although van Heusen wrote music mainly for film and the stage, his rich use of melody, harmony and complex bass lines makes his work ideal for jazz musicians like pianist Jackman, bassist Jones and drummer Brooks. The musical format of the jazz piano trio, which developed during the modern jazz era of the 1940s and 1950s, flourished in Oakland and the East Bay during the 1950s, most famously with the Dave Brubeck trio — but has since nearly disappeared. In fact, In the Tradition is the last classic jazz piano trio — with a piano, bass and drums — still active in the East Bay. Bill Jackman, playing with the trio for the past 30 years, was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher, who for several decades presided over the grand piano at the former Solomon Grundy’s (now Skates) on the Berkeley Marina. Jackman is also a Lupita Records musician who has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader who has played throughout the Bay Area for over 30 years. After studying music at the University of Northern Colorado, he moved to the Bay Area in the mid-1970s, where he played with many icons including Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders and Buddy Montgomery. As a sideman and bandleader, Jones has served as the music director for the Golden Gate Library Summer Concert and Jam Session series in Oakland for the past 23 years. Dr. Albert Brooks grew up dancing to Latin music in the South Bronx, playing these rhythms on any percussion instrument he could get his hands on. Alongside Latin drumming, he added trap drums to his musical offerings several decades ago and fluently melds these with swing rhythms. He has juggled his growth as a drummer with the demands of being a practicing obstetrician-gynecologist in the East Bay for nearly 30 years, having graduated in 1974 from the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University in New York City. Tickets ($25) for the show at PCA (801 Magnolia Ave.) are available at bpt.me/6214927. This Sunday In the Tradition Piano Trio will pay tribute to composer Jimmy van Heusen at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

articles.text: The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra program at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday was very interesting. The takeaway was: “Music is needed… Now more than ever.” Music director Jory Fankuchen spoke eloquently on the matter. The event began with a table, elegantly set with delectable things to eat. This put us all in a very good mindset. What came next was the musical portion of the program featuring a string quartet playing a wide variety of audience-pleasing music. You would expect the music to be thoroughly professional in quality; and it was. We heard selections from Haydn, Tchaikovsky, and Dvořák. Everybody was in a good mood. Violist and composer Darcy Rindt, the Executive Director of San Francisco Chamber Orchestra took the podium and began the introductions. She thanked all of the supporters for their generous contributions and looked forward to future successes. Then she introduced music director and conductor Jory Fankuchen in a fascinating one-on-one interview. The questions were well thought out as were the responses. It is important at this time to take stock of why music is important in our society – now more than ever. Fankuchen was very clear in declaring that the orchestra would maintain high standards of performance and that no admission will be charged at any time. “Fill the seats.” These are very good principles, but I would like to suggest a few other things. First is the realization that school administrators continue to cut music education in our society. They fail to realize a very simple human characteristic. We need music in all aspects of our lives. When I was a teacher in public schools, I went to every classroom and introduced music to the kids. The first thing I told them was “music is fun”. Music is as good as any sport and the good thing is there are no injuries. Everyone learns to be a good sportsman and have respect in all aspects. Yes, music teaches these things. By playing music you just get smarter and learn problem-solving. Prejudice does not exist in music. You get to travel and see other cultures. Perhaps the most important thing is that is the value you get. When I was a teacher in the public schools, I saw approximately 1200 students every week. That’s a pretty good value don’t you think? May I suggest at this time that my readers contact their school administrators? Many years ago, I was the concertmaster of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra. The conductor at that time was the founder Edgar Braun. He was the most open-minded and generous musician I have ever known. It is because of him that I achieved an international music career. This put us all in a very good mindset. What came next was the musical portion of the program featuring a string quartet playing a wide variety of audience-pleasing music. You would expect the music to be thoroughly professional in quality; and it was. We heard selections from Haydn, Tchaikovsky, and Dvořák. Everybody was in a good mood. Violist and composer Darcy Rindt, the Executive Director of San Francisco Chamber Orchestra took the podium and began the introductions. She thanked all of the supporters for their generous contributions and looked forward to future successes. Then she introduced music director and conductor Jory Fankuchen in a fascinating one-on-one interview. The questions were well thought out as were the responses. It is important at this time to take stock of why music is important in our society – now more than ever. Fankuchen was very clear in declaring that the orchestra would maintain high standards of performance and that no admission will be charged at any time. “Fill the seats.” These are very good principles, but I would like to suggest a few other things. First is the realization that school administrators continue to cut music education in our society. They fail to realize a very simple human characteristic. We need music in all aspects of our lives. When I was a teacher in public schools, I went to every classroom and introduced music to the kids. The first thing I told them was “music is fun”. Music is as good as any sport and the good thing is there are no injuries. Everyone learns to be a good sportsman and have respect in all aspects. Yes, music teaches these things. By playing music you just get smarter and learn problem-solving. Prejudice does not exist in music. You get to travel and see other cultures. Perhaps the most important thing is that is the value you get. When I was a teacher in the public schools, I saw approximately 1200 students every week. That’s a pretty good value don’t you think? May I suggest at this time that my readers contact their school administrators? Many years ago, I was the concertmaster of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra. François Pinault, the second richest mogul in France, says he has collected at least 10,000 pieces of contemporary art. He persisted for two decades to get Parisians interested in trying out more edgy art to infuse the city’s museums and gallery scene. Now the timing is right. articles.text: It’s art, and it’s distinctly contemporary. The show features the work of 32 artists on the ground level. Take the stairs up to see more galleries. Ouverture runs through December 31. Placards are in English and French. The Bourse renovation was in tandem with its interior redesign to partition spaces into galleries arranged around the Rotunda. Two hundred years ago the site was an exchange for trading grain commodities. More recently, the Bourse de Commerce was the Paris stock exchange, but it closed in 1998 rather than ease into the digital era. Further back in history, Catherine de’ Medici’s palace stood here, and a vestigial column remains as an historical marker. The building’s elegant circular design dates to the 18th century after it evolved from being a granary with a wooden roof. articles.text: It was still hot on October 7th when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion, so they assembled inside the Community Hall. There was a good turnout of 17 readers on hand. Discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus couldn’t be with them, so Dick Carter, who had suggested this month’s book, led the conversation. Before they got started on their discussion, it was shared that there will be a Piedmont Adult Recreation Expo on Sunday, November 17th, from 2 to 4:30 PM at the Veterans Building. Representatives from groups that provide recreation in Piedmont for adults, including the reading group, will be there to tell attendees about their activities and how to get involved. The book for this day’s discussion was Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell. The author wants us to better understand the world of “outliers.” These are the best and the brightest, the most famous and the most successful people. What makes them different? Gladwell says we pay too much attention to what successful people are like, and too little attention to where they are from. He explains why some people become software billionaires, what it takes to be a great soccer player, why Asians are good at math, and what made the Beatles the greatest rock band. Gladwell believes the idea of the “self-made man” is a myth, and that once you reach a certain threshold, increased abilities no longer help you succeed. He says world-class mastery of anything demands around 10,000 hours of practice. The month and year you’re born in can have a huge effect on what you achieve. How you are raised can radically impact how successful you become. Where you’re from geographically and culturally is important for success and recognizing it can prevent failure. Gladwell contends if we understand this, we can create more opportunities for people to succeed. The readers generally liked Outliers. They found it interesting and easy to read, and agreed Gladwell is an excellent storyteller. They liked his premise and could relate to the different stories and the lessons he is trying to communicate. The book provides a fuller picture of what is going on in life, and the group could personally relate to examples Gladwell presents. They knew of “redshirting kindergarteners” where parents hold their children back a year so they can be the oldest and most mature members of their classes. It was also helpful to understand cultural environments, and how junior Korean pilots would be reluctant to voice a concern to their older co-pilots with disastrous consequences. There was a significant backlash to the book. While some readers liked some aspects of the book, they didn’t care for others. Gladwell mainly presents others’ research, and they felt he cherry picks examples and research that supports his positions. Gladwell recognizes outliers are talented people, but it seemed underplayed to some, as is just plain luck and being in the right place at the right time. What would Bill Gates have been if he didn’t have a high school situation that let him have practically unlimited access to computer programming time? Probably successful too. Other interesting questions also came out of the conversation. The success of Chinese Olympic divers, who are identified at a very young age and do little else for the next 10 plus years of their lives, raised the question, do we need diverse educations or just concentrated study for success? Bob Hall observed that the group will have the opportunity to learn more about the factors behind the success of four American presidents in the group’s selection of Leadership: In Turbulent Times by historian Doris Kearns Goodwin as the selection for December. The readers had also previously selected North Woods by Danile Mason for November. After hearing reviews of three fiction possibilities, the group selected the classic A Farewell to Arms by Ernest Hemingway for the first book of 2025. The group’s next discussion will be on November 4 at 1:30 PM. Weather permitting, it will be outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join and there is no fee. Register at https:// bit.ly/3R86PP4. Participants at the First Mondays Reading Group gathering on October 7 included Albert Chen, Adrienne Hamlin, Judy Love, Ken Young, Darby and Gerry Gregg, Laura Goldman, Carol Long, Bob Hall, Nancy Henn, Claudine Bach, Martin Levy, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Melba Yee, Mike Henn, Karin Fetherston, and Dick Carter.

We enjoy this seasonal favorite countless times throughout fall and winter. Creating dishes using minimal ingredients with maximal taste is the key in these days of home cooking. A spice blend will do the heavy lifting on seasoning this dish. It’s the key behind this five-ingredient recipe. In addition to a chile blend, I’ve prepared versions of roasted vegetables using curry blends, harissa, Ras el Hanout, and Chinese Five Spice. You get to take your pick. This recipe has endless adaptations with vegetables, aromatics, spices and herbs. I happen to have a favorite spicery where I’ve purchased freshly milled herbs, chiles, and spices for years, Local Spicery. It’s important to like the spice blends right out of the jar to minimize fussing and doctoring them to suit your taste buds. The idea is that they make things easy, so go with a brand that works for you. There is no shortage of local spice shops for that personal touch, and there is an abundant variety of spice blends at local markets. Any flavor profile you enjoy will work here. So will a simple dusting of sea salt and freshly ground pepper. Five ingredients deliver an outstanding result. F-I-V-E! Chile Roasted Brussels Sprouts and Delicata Squash Makes about four cups INGREDIENTS • 1 pound Brussels sprouts, deep green, sliced in half lengthwise • 1 pound delicata squash, ends trimmed, halved and seeds removed; sliced into 1/2-inch thick pieces • 1 tablespoon olive oil • 1 tablespoon chile powder blend, or substitute any preferred spice blend • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste if your spice blend is salt-free INSTRUCTIONS Place an oven rack on the middle rack of the oven and preheat the oven to either 350° F on the “convection-roast” setting, or 400° F on the “bake” setting. Place the sliced Brussels sprouts and delicata squash on a sheet pan and drizzle with 1 tablespoons of olive oil. Stir the Brussels sprouts and squash pieces around to cover each with olive oil. Add more oil if needed. Arrange the slices into a single layer. Place the pan of Brussels sprouts and squash into the oven and roast for about 12 – 15 minutes, when you see some browning on them, remove the pan from the oven. Using a spatula, move the pieces close together and sprinkle with chile powder blend (or other spice blend) and salt to taste. Stir to mix, then spread out into an even layer and return the pan to the oven. Roast an additional 5 – 7 minutes until both the Brussels sprouts and squash are golden-brown. Test the vegetables with a fork to check they are tender but still provide slight resistance. You don’t want them mushy. Walkers take a stroll on Kingston and Rose By Dick Carter The heat wave finally broke last Wednesday, just in time for the Walking on Wednesdays group’s weekly walk. They decided to see Rose and Kingston Avenues on for the first time this year. These streets are some of Piedmont’s earliest with many old homes and some beautiful Victorians. The group headed off going down Highland Avenue to Park Way. onto Ramona and Ronada Avenues to Grand Avenue just before it becomes Oakland’s Pleasant Valley Road at Moraga Avenue. The walkers couldn’t resist walking the rarely visited Parkside Drive cul-de-sac. Then, it was across Grand Avenue and on to Rose Avenue to where homes on the right side are in Oakland and homes on the left are in Piedmont. They enjoyed seeing Rose’s many old, lovely homes that were built between 1890 and 1930. They went past three especially charming Victorians on Rose, including one dating to 1895. Then they crossed Linda to go up Kingston. In this 700 block of Kingston the homes on the north side are also in Oakland and the homes on the south side are in Piedmont. To their surprise on Kingston they saw walker and local historian Meghan Bennett, who grew up at 780 Kingston. Research by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombard provided the story of Meghan’s old home and that of the house next door at 778. These two homes were built in 1892 by William Vickery and his sister, Elizabeth Vickery Hadden, at costs of $4,300 and $3,300. They were the first homes on the street which was then called Summit Avenue. Meghan shared an article from a 1904 issue of the Oakland Enquirer that said 10 property owners had sent a petition to the City Council asking to change the street’s name from Summit to Kingston. These houses were built in the fashionable shingle style of the 1890s. The backyard of the house at 778 is one of the deepest lots in Piedmont, 220 feet deep. Google Maps shows the backyard of the home at 784 is even deeper. Neighborhood lore says the two houses once shared a kitchen and the two families ate their meals together. There are many wonderful homes on Kingston, but the classic Victoria at 836 is one of the best. It was built in 1885 on nearby Monte Vista Avenue in Oakland and moved one block in 1910 to its current location. Nancy DeRoche wanted the group to see an historic brick home a little further up Kingston that was designed by Albert Farr, built in 1908m and currently occupied by Chad Olcott and Laura Pochop, owners of Mulberry’s Market. Going to the far reaches of Piedmont was a longer walk than usual, and it was time for them to make their return to the Exedra. They went back up Kingston, down Greenbank Avenue, across Grand Avenue, up to Oakland, El Cerrito, and Magnolia Avenues. They had a good, long walk with wonderful, old homes, some history, and lots of friends on a lovely morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register ar https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. A strong turnout of 51 walkers and five K-9 best friends showed up for a walk to Rose and Kingston Avenues. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission met at City Hall on Monday, October 14, to analyze a pair of draft plans for two possible build sites related to the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Prior to the meeting, University of California professor and Piedmont resident Ralph Catalano raised concerns that sight distances for vehicles on roads in the proposed area of construction did not comply with Caltrans safety guidelines. Catalano urged city officials not to make a decision on the proposed plans until a comprehensive review of sight lines and stopping distances are conducted to ensure the highest degree of public safety. The commission noted that the Monday meeting was a study session held as a preliminary step prior to the completion of a draft specific plan. The completed draft plan is expected by city officials to be released for public review and comment in late 2024. During the meeting, members of the Piedmont Planning Commission reviewed landscape design requirements for new multifamily housing and requirements for public services, utilities and infrastructure in the proposed build area for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Among the priorities and considerations for the commission regarding the project were construction with the existing landscape of Moraga Canyon to encourage the siting of future development, enacting architectural standards that integrate building design, access and site improvements for market-rate and affordable multifamily developments and providing flexibility in building and land use design while describing Piedmont’s and it residents’ preferences for future development. The commission noted that final determination of the build plan will rely heavily on contractor input to ensure that the city of Piedmont gets the best available deal when undertaking the construction project. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is a construction effort by the city to comply with a state mandate for more housing by incorporating between 132 and 199 units of new housing, 60 units of which are slated to be reserved for households earning lower incomes. The city anticipates the project to include development of multifamily residential buildings that would stand between four and six stories in the canyon. The project is studying all cityowned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park and the city’s Corporation Yard. The city owns five parcels of land totaling about 18 acres on both the north and south sides of Moraga Avenue near Red Rock Road. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan also seeks to develop detailed methods to maintain and improve existing city facilities, recreational amenities and open space and improve bicycle, pedestrian and traffic safety. The plan also seeks to enhance wildfire safety and evacuation protocols. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, October 16, 2024 Planning Commission reviews Moraga Canyon housing options By Andrew Fortin-Caldera The Piedmont Planning Commission met at City Hall on Monday, October 14, to analyze a pair of draft plans for two possible build sites related to the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Prior to the meeting, University of California professor and Piedmont resident Ralph Catalano raised concerns that sight distances for vehicles on roads in the proposed area of construction did not comply with Caltrans safety guidelines. Catalano urged city officials not to make a decision on the proposed plans until a comprehensive review of sight lines and stopping distances are conducted to ensure the highest degree of public safety. The commission noted that the Monday meeting was a study session held as a preliminary step prior to the completion of a draft specific plan. The completed draft plan is expected by city officials to be released for public review and comment in late 2024. During the meeting, members of the Piedmont Planning Commission reviewed landscape design requirements for new multifamily housing and requirements for public services, utilities and infrastructure in the proposed build area for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Among the priorities and considerations for the commission regarding the project were construction with the existing landscape of Moraga Canyon to encourage the siting of future development, enacting architectural standards that integrate building design, access and site improvements for market-rate and affordable multifamily developments and providing flexibility in building and land use design while describing Piedmont’s and it residents’ preferences for future development. The commission noted that final determination of the build plan will rely heavily on contractor input to ensure that the city of Piedmont gets the best available deal when undertaking the construction project. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is a construction effort by the city to comply with a state mandate for more housing by incorporating between 132 and 199 units of new housing, 60 units of which are slated to be reserved for households earning lower incomes. The city anticipates the project to include development of multifamily residential buildings that would stand between four and six stories in the canyon. The project is studying all cityowned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park and the city’s Corporation Yard. The city owns five parcels of land totaling about 18 acres on both the north and south sides of Moraga Avenue near Red Rock Road. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan also seeks to develop detailed methods to maintain and improve existing city facilities, recreational amenities and open space and improve bicycle, pedestrian and traffic safety. The plan also seeks to enhance wildfire safety and evacuation protocols.
